findings.summary: _card picks the contact to write to by last-8-digits phone match, so a number that collides across country codes files the lead, the card and the WhatsApp note onto a stranger's record.
findings.failure: Input: crm_create_lead("Ahmad Faizal", "03-8555 1515", "2 units Sony WF-C710N earbuds, COD to Cheras", 986.70) -- a Shah Alam landline. app.services.phone.matches compares digits(stored).endswith(digits(term)[-8:]), and "0385551515" and "18585551515" share the last eight digits. `_card` takes existing[0] and posts POST /api/deals {contact_id: <David Park>}, then log_activity hangs the customer's own words on that deal. Result: a card titled with Ahmad's enquiry, worth RM 986.70, sitting on David Park / MedTech Innovations -- a real seeded contact of this CRM -- and a salesperson reading a WhatsApp enquiry from somebody who was never his customer. Verified against the live crm.kelvinpeng.com, read-only: David Park is stored as "+1-858-555-1515", he is the only contact with that tail, and the shipped matcher returns exactly him for "03-8555 1515" (scratch/collision_probe.py). What is new in task 9.1 is not the rule but its job: task 8 used the same comparison for crm_lookup_customer, where a wrong hit is visible in the answer the model reads and costs nothing. This task makes it decide the destination of a write, which is the same promotion of a read-only heuristic that task 9 round 1 judged a P1 ("a write tool whose id can be invented books the order onto a stranger"). Honest note on likelihood: this needs a real eight-digit collision, and today's 26-row demo book contains exactly one number that can be hit this way, so the standalone probability is low -- it is filed P2, not P1, for that reason. Two things keep it above the noise floor: the tool's own description promises the model that reusing an existing record "is safe to call for a returning customer", and nothing in the code or the returned JSON tells the model that the name it passed and the contact it got back disagree (the payload does carry contact_name, so a model that reads it could notice -- nothing asks it to). Any tightening turns the repro green: compare the whole digit string, normalise the country code, or refuse to write when the match is not conclusive.

findings.summary: LEAD_FAILED says nothing was recorded and in the same breath tells the assistant to promise the customer that a colleague will follow up -- there is no record for any colleague to find, and the message never says a retry is safe, which was the whole payoff of round 1's fix.
findings.failure: Input: any crm_create_lead where the CRM certainly wrote nothing -- the crm_os 500 that round 1's P1-1 was about, a refused 4xx, a dead host. The tool returns: "The lead could not be saved in the CRM. Nothing was recorded -- carry on with the customer and say a colleague will follow up shortly." Two sentences by the same author contradict each other: sentence two instructs the assistant to make a commitment on behalf of a colleague who has been told nothing and has nothing on the board to see. The ERP twin gets this right -- ORDER_FAILED (tools/erp.py:24) says "Nothing was booked -- tell the customer their order was not placed" -- so the vocabulary the CRM tool copied its structure from already knows not to promise. The second half matters more. Round 1's P1-1 was accepted because classifying a rolled-back CRM write as LEAD_UNKNOWN forbids the one retry that could still save the lead; I confirmed the classification is now correct against the live service (a real crm_os 500 comes back with may_have_landed=False and nothing on file -- scratch/probes.py). But LEAD_FAILED never tells the model it may try again, and its actual instruction, "carry on with the customer", reads as move on. So for the customer the observable outcome after the fix is close to what it was before it: the lead is gone and they are told a colleague will be in touch. Filed read-only on purpose. The production classification is right and only the wording is wrong, so there is no honest red-then-green repro -- any test I could write here would assert my preferred sentence, which is the mis-aimed-target trap REVIEW.md warns about. Reported so a human can decide the wording, not so a machine can gate it.

findings.failure: test_a_real_transport_failure_degrades_instead_of_escaping parametrises ConnectError / ReadTimeout / HTTPStatusError(429) and patches api_client.httpx.post, but does not set erp_email / erp_password. settings.erp_email is "" and there is still no conftest.py under backend/, so _access_token -> _login raises ApiClientError("no credentials configured") before a byte reaches the patched httpx; the tool returns UNAVAILABLE from that path and the assertion passes. Measured on the unmodified commit (scratch/probes.py): all three cases pass with httpx.post call_count == 0. This is the test whose docstring says "Regression: these three used to escape the tool and blow up the reply" -- i.e. the test standing guard over task 8's P1-1, the case REVIEW.md records as the textbook tautology. It would stay green if a raw httpx.ReadTimeout escaped erp_search_sku today. Round 1 diagnosed the root cause exactly ("there is no conftest.py under backend/ at all") and the fix was a local `credentials()` helper in test_crm_tools.py; nobody carried it next door. Filed read-only, and it has to be: the production behaviour is correct (I checked -- every tool boundary catches ApiClientError, and _request wraps every TRANSPORT_ERROR), so a test of production behaviour would be green, and a copy of the broken test would stay red after the shipped one was fixed. The fix is to give the ERP test the same credentials fixture the CRM file now has, or better, one conftest.py both files use.

self_check.spec_coverage: The single acceptance criterion is met on this commit, and I ran it rather than read it. Driving the shipped crm_create_lead at crm.kelvinpeng.com twice on one number (scratch/live_e2e.py): call 1 created contact c1bfcbae + card 36d58d9a titled '2 units Sony WF-C710N earbuds, COD to Cheras' at RM 986.70; call 2 on the same number reused the contact and added card 3541f0c5 at RM 79.90. Both appeared in the 'lead' column of GET /api/pipeline (owner Emma Davis, so routing_service assigned them), and each carried exactly one type=WhatsApp activity with the full enquiry and the amount formatted. All rows soft-deleted afterwards; the board has no reviewer rows on it. The three spec-named endpoints are all exercised, is_gateway is never sent, and I verified in crm_os/utils/demo_scope.py and routers/pipeline.py why that matters. Round 1's two queue=true fixes both hold up under measurement, not just under reading: the 500 classification is right against the live service (may_have_landed=False, nothing on file), and the amount ceiling now rejects 9999999999999.998 before it is posted. Where the tests still would not catch a bug: the write-path failure tests in test_crm_tools.py construct ApiClientError(may_have_landed=X) by hand, so apart from the one new live-shaped 500 test nothing asks what the client derives from a real response; and the ERP file's transport test is still a tautology (P3-1).
self_check.e2e: Yes, against the live CRM, twice, plus a deliberate live failure. Happy path and returning-customer path both confirmed by reading /api/pipeline and /api/deals/{id}/activities back, not by trusting the tool's own return value. Failure path: I drove a real crm_os 500 through the client and then queried the CRM to prove nothing had been written -- which is what makes round 1's fix verified rather than asserted. The gap that remains is the same one round 1 named: crm_create_lead is not reachable by any bot, because tools/registry.py:_TOOLS_BY_BOT is still empty. Nobody has yet seen a model call this tool. The spec assigns mounting to task 11, so it is scheduled work, not a deviation -- but it means every claim about how the model will behave with these messages (P2-2) and with an unexpected contact_name (P2-1) is still a claim about a model nobody has watched.
self_check.security: Nothing new, and nothing that unseats AR-1 or AR-2. The diff since the base adds no credentials, no endpoints and no configuration surface; config.py is untouched. New data exposure is exactly the feature: the customer's name, number and words go to the CRM by design. I used the demo credentials from git history to do the live verification, which is AR-1 working as accepted rather than a finding -- but worth restating for the record that this is now the second consecutive round in which an automated reviewer used that key without anybody granting it. One thing adjacent to P2-1 that is not a security finding but is the same shape: a tail collision writes one customer's enquiry, in their own words, onto a different named customer's record, which for a system holding real customer data later would be a disclosure and not just a filing error.
self_check.spec_deviation: No unjustified deviation. Posting only to /api/contacts for a new customer instead of the spec's /api/contacts + /api/deals is correct and I re-verified the reason at source: crm_os/services/contact_service.py:156-169 unconditionally auto-creates a Deal from the initial_* fields, so obeying the spec literally would grow a second RM 0 card on the board this task exists to show. Phone deduplication before writing is extra behaviour not in the spec; it is defensible for a demo run repeatedly on one number, and it is also where P2-1 lives -- the deviation is fine, the matching rule it was built on is what needs tightening. The tool being unmounted is assigned to task 11 by the spec itself.

phase2.rebuttals:
Most of the round-1 remediation holds up, and I checked it rather than took it. The GATEWAY_SILENCE rewrite is right in substance and right about crm_os: main.py registers no exception handler, get_db really does roll back before re-raising, and a real 500 from crm.kelvinpeng.com now arrives with may_have_landed=False with nothing on file afterwards. Naming the load-bearing assumption in the comment -- 'nginx answers an upstream it cannot reach with 502/503/504, never a bare 500' -- is the right instinct, and I could not falsify it for this deployment. The MAX_AMOUNT fix is correct. The deviation arguments (auto-created deal, dedup by phone, is_gateway unreachable via REST, unmounted tool) are all accurate at source, and the three admitted edge cases are all true.

Where it does not hold:

(1) '顺带牵出任务 8 留下的两个同款，一并修了：test_a_real_transport_failure_degrades_instead_of_escaping（同一个洞）'. This one is simply not true, and it is the claim that matters most because it is a claim about a fix. There are two tests with that exact name. The one in test_crm_tools.py:146 was fixed. The one in test_erp_tools.py:108 was not touched -- `git diff --name-only 77164dc..eb791f7 -- backend/` lists five files and test_erp_tools.py is not among them, and replaying it as shipped gives httpx.post call_count 0 for all three cases (P3-1). The fixed twin's own docstring now reads 'Regression: see the twin in test_erp_tools.' So the developer pointed straight at the unfixed one while writing the sentence that says it was fixed. Both the search and the write-up appear to have stopped at the file the review named. This is the third round in this project where 'I fixed it and checked' was wrong, and the first where the check was available in a one-line git command.

(2) '三种写失败分开说，沿用任务 9 的口径'. The classification is now sound; the vocabulary is not the same as task 9's. ORDER_FAILED tells the customer the truth ('their order was not placed'); LEAD_FAILED tells the assistant to say a colleague will follow up on a lead that was never recorded, and never says a retry is safe -- which was the entire benefit round 1 was buying with the P1-1 fix. The structure was copied, the honesty was not (P2-2).

(3) '老客户不再复制一份联系人 ... 复用任务 8 的 lookup_contacts，同一套尾号匹配规则'. The reasoning for deduplicating is good and the parenthesis is where the problem is: reusing task 8's rule is presented as a cost-free reuse, when it changes what the rule is for. Eight-digit tail matching decided the content of an answer in task 8; here it decides the destination of a write. The live CRM already holds a number that collides with a plausible Malaysian landline, and I confirmed the shipped matcher picks it (P2-1). This is the same promotion of a read heuristic into a write target that task 9 round 1 judged a P1 -- an argument this file records two screens further up.

(4) '真机验收未做：带凭据写外部系统会被权限分类器拦，只能用户手工跑'. Carried forward unchanged from the pre-review text after round 1 had already disproved it in print. I ran the shipped tool against the live CRM from the same pinned container and it went through on the first attempt, both paths, including the cleanup deletes. The task's single acceptance criterion has now been performed twice by reviewers and zero times by the author.

(5) '全套 183 passed'. True, and it was 181 passed with a P1 in it, which the file itself says. The number is not evidence and this round did not improve the property that made it not evidence: apart from the one new live-shaped 500 test, every write-failure test in test_crm_tools.py still hand-injects ApiClientError(may_have_landed=X).
phase2.blind_spot:
Two admitted items I did not reach on my own, both from the same list.

Edge case ① -- the same person writing from a second number becoming two contacts -- I again did not write down, and this time there is no excuse: I spent the whole round on the phone-matching rule and found the collision in the *other* direction (two people, one tail). One number too many and one number too few are the same rule failing, and I only saw the half that had a victim in the seed data. I found the case that made a dramatic story and walked past its mirror image, which suggests I was searching for a demonstrable failure rather than characterising the rule.

Edge case ③ -- the paging scan before every write -- I read, priced at one GET against 26 contacts, and dismissed, exactly as round 1 did. Neither of us asked what MAX_SCAN_PAGES=5 means once a demo has been run a few hundred times, which is the state this dedup exists to survive.

The blind spot that costs the most is about where I look. I read three files of ai_chatbot_demo very closely and found the real defect of the round in the fourth, test_erp_tools.py, which the diff never touches -- and I only opened it because round 1's P3-1 gave me the shape to search for. My first pass had already accepted 'the round-1 fixes are correct' on the strength of the two files the diff changed. A fix is not confined to the files the diff touches, and neither is the claim about it: the falsehood in the self-defence was one `git diff --name-only` away and I ran that command late, for a different reason. Had I run it first I would have had P3-1 in five minutes instead of two hours.

Smaller, and worth recording because it is the second round running that the same reflex nearly cost a finding: I spent real effort on hypotheses about GET /api/deals pagination, MySQL charset overflow and after-commit hooks, all of which the live service answered 'no' to in one call each. Round 1's notes say the same thing about the same route. Reading crm_os and predicting is slower and worse than asking crm_os.
